On Linux NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability 8.0 or newer, the float32 consumer restore can fuse the existing colour operations and quantization into one channels-last write. This is on by default wherever Triton and a host C compiler are present — torch's CUDA wheel already selects a Triton, so an existing `device_hsv` run there takes the fused path without installing anything (`uv pip install -e ".[cuda-hsv]"` adds Triton where it is missing). `--data.fused_hsv false` keeps `device_hsv` on the native CUDA restore, to step around a toolchain or bisect a difference between the two. The first call compiles the kernel and needs a host C compiler. The extra also installs the existing Setuptools build dependency needed by older Triton SDKs. A Triton `ImportError`, a missing compiler, other devices, noncontiguous buffers and other consumer precisions retain the native restore. So does a first compile or launch that fails: it warns once with its cause, and the native restore runs for the rest of the process. Gain sampling, rounding and the uint8 boundary are unchanged. Direct `unpack_batch` calls keep their existing path.

This can help a CPU-limited training run, including one with decoded images cached by `--data.cache_train_images true`. It transports float32 images until the colour transform finishes, so image IPC and host-to-device bytes are four times the default uint8 transport. The shared-memory worker cap budgets float32 images only when the module chooses the worker count (`--data.num_workers` unset) in one process; segmentation masks still need their own memory allowance. A named `--data.num_workers` is neither capped nor warned: batch 64 at 640 px with 8 workers and `prefetch_factor` 2 queues about 5.0 GB of `/dev/shm` in float32, against 1.26 GB in uint8. Each DDP rank budgets the free `/dev/shm` on its own, so ranks sharing one host can jointly overcommit it — a known limit. The cap cannot shrink a batch: with a small `/dev/shm`, enlarge it or use `--data.num_workers 0`. Measure the complete run on the intended host.

## Prepare the next epoch during validation

`--data.epoch_prefetch true` with `--data.persistent_workers true` lets the existing workers prepare up to `num_workers x prefetch_factor` batches of the next training epoch during the last step and validation. It is opt-in because the training queue can remain resident alongside validation inputs: `num_workers x prefetch_factor` batches of host memory, about 1.26 GB of uint8 images for the batch 64, 640 px, 8 worker, `prefetch_factor` 2 example above, or about 5.0 GB of float32 with `--data.device_hsv true`. With pinned host memory, which is on by default when CUDA is available, queued batches can sit in page-locked RAM that the `/dev/shm` worker cap does not budget. Use it when dataset and augmentation configuration remain stable between epochs. Every packaged config breaks that: its `CloseMosaicCallback` switches mosaic off for the final epochs through `set_mosaic_prob`, which persistent workers never see, because each keeps the pipeline copy it started with — those epochs would still train on mosaics. The module warns once when such a change arrives under `epoch_prefetch`; keep `--data.persistent_workers false` for these configs. It applies to full, single-CUDA epochs with the module's own shuffle generator; batch limits, a step bound, overfit, loader reloads and distributed training keep the ordinary loader, as do non-persistent workers, and the run warns once naming the first unmet condition. CUDA is the boundary because the overlap was measured only on one CUDA GPU (an L4); other accelerators are unmeasured, not known to fail. The configured final epoch does not prepare another one. Measure the complete fit: the benefit is greatest when first-batch preparation is a meaningful fraction of the epoch.

## Decoded training-image cache

`--data.cache_train_images true` decodes each distinct training file name during datamodule setup and keeps the RGB `uint8` tensor in host RAM. Mosaic, affine, colour and flip augmentation still run on fresh float storage for every draw; only the repeated JPEG/PNG decode disappears. COCO and YOLO training readers support the flag, and validation is deliberately not cached.

Budget the option from the uncompressed images, not their files: approximately `sum(3 * height * width)` bytes for 8-bit sources, before Python/tensor metadata — a 16-bit PNG decodes to `uint16` and costs two bytes per channel, so twice that — and once per device: a multi-GPU run spawns one process per rank, each building its own `DetectionDataModule` and therefore its own cache, so the single-process budget above multiplies by `trainer.devices`. The cache is keyed by file name (by path for the YOLO reader), so two records naming one file share an entry, while the same picture stored under two names is decoded and held twice. It defaults off.

Whether DataLoader workers share the cache depends on the multiprocessing start method, not on the operating system, and the data module leaves the start method at the platform default. Under `fork` the workers read the parent's cache through copy-on-write pages, so it costs one copy of RAM however many workers there are. Under `spawn` and `forkserver` — the default on macOS and Windows, and on Linux from Python 3.14 — the cache is pickled to every worker, torch moves each cached tensor into shared memory to do it (one segment or file descriptor per image), and with `--data.persistent_workers false`, the default, the hand-over repeats every epoch. The values are identical either way; a non-fork start method does not promise the one-copy cost or the speedup, and a large split can meet file-descriptor or `/dev/shm` limits at a size nobody has measured. The pipeline never writes to the cache — every draw converts into fresh float storage. Leave it off when the split does not fit comfortably beside the loader queue, model, optimizer and operating-system cache.

### Prepared training-source cache

`--data.cache_prepared_train_images true` also reuses float conversion and affine centring before random augmentation. It takes precedence over `cache_train_images`, keeps one float32 source per training record and snapshots YOLO labels with their images. Mosaic, geometry, colour, targets and RNG draws keep their existing results. The option defaults off.

Budget about `12 * sum(height * width)` bytes for the retained RGB pixels, plus target and reader metadata, per training process. Extrapolated from the 1,024-image slice measured in [WP-192c](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-192c/) (3.30 MB per image), the full COCO train2017 split would need about 390 GB per process; this is an extrapolation, not a measured run. Every DDP rank is a separate process and holds its own copy, so ranks on one host multiply that figure. Each float32 pixel channel uses four times the bytes of an 8-bit channel. The prepared cache retains separate images for duplicate COCO records, whereas the decoded cache deduplicates file names. COCO reports an estimate before decoding; YOLO has no annotation sizes and reports the retained pixel bytes afterwards. Under `spawn` or `forkserver` (see above), workers receive cached tensors through shared memory, so budget the cache alongside the queued batches. Forked workers share its read-only pages. Fit-stage setup builds the cache once, repeated fit setup reuses it, and other stages release the datamodule's references. Measure the complete fit on the intended host.

## Independent segmentation predictions

`--model.capture_segment_heads true --trainer.precision bf16-mixed` records the existing segmentation prediction routines, including their first-order backward work. The default is `false`. Box/class stems remain independent; coefficients, prototypes and semantic logits have separate backward nodes so an empty mask objective keeps absent gradients. With this option alone, common features, prototype fusion, assignment, losses, state updates and schedules stay native. Enable `capture_network` separately to replay the common features too.

Byte-exact agreement with native training is verified only on NVIDIA L4 (sm_89) with torch 2.9.1+cu129; other GPUs and torch builds are unverified. The route requires PyTorch 2.9 or newer, one CUDA device and automatic optimisation. Gradient accumulation replays too ([WP-208](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-208/)): a live gradient is copied out of a group's recorded gradient buffers at forward time, before the replay that would overwrite them, as network replay does. CPU, MPS, FP32, FP16 and older BF16 runtimes warn and use native calls; evaluation stays native too. Custom or changed prediction dispatch, hooks, frozen prediction parameters, aliased storage and retained feature gradients retire replay for the fit. Each prediction group records one input signature per fit (shape, stride, dtype, device, gradient flag and CUDA stream); a call with any other signature, a partial batch included, runs the native head without adding another graph, and the recorded graph pools stay reserved until the fit ends, so a run whose batch shapes keep changing pays that memory without replaying. Copying, checkpoints and fit teardown retain the original parameter names and no recording.

A recording failure raises after restoring running buffers and RNG state; disable the flag to keep that run native. The flag retains CUDA graph pools, so check reserved memory and throughput on the actual batch size. A replayed step's mask coefficients, prototypes and semantic logits live in CUDA graph memory that the next replay overwrites in place; box and class predictions are copies. Anything that keeps those three tensors, or a gradient adopted from their backward, beyond the training step that produced them has to clone it. Measurements and rejected alternatives belong to [WP-193e](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193e/#wp-193e); a small-batch result does not establish a large-batch speed-up.

## Opt-in CUDA network replay

`--model.capture_network true` records the detection backbone, neck and dual head with PyTorch's `make_graphed_callables`, including their backward pass. Assignment, losses, optimizer, LR/alpha schedules and EMA keep the ordinary loop. It is separate from `compile_step` and cannot be combined with that flag. The default is `false`. The measured speed-up is limited to a small-batch workload (batch 4); batch-32 screens changed direction, so check throughput on your own batch size before enabling it.

For `task: keypoints`, the same flag records backbone and neck plus eighteen independent box/class/point stems through the private prediction runner. Each point stem has its own backward node: a batch with no assigned positives keeps its point-parameter gradients absent. The current RLE/OKS or Laplace objectives stay native. A fully frozen backbone and neck, changed head topology or dispatch, and head hooks/compilation keep pose native; a partial shared-feature freeze still replays. A fully frozen start or a later change to the shared-feature trainable set keeps the rest of the fit native after one warning. Changing a stem's trainable set or module mode retires that stem's recording, with a warning naming the stem; replacing a head module retires the parent before feature replay. The measured benefit is for nano/640/BF16, batch 4 on L4: five complete pairs save 12.97%, including setup, validation and checkpoints, against the existing shared-feature replay. Reserved memory rises from 1384 to 1730 MiB. Check time and memory on another batch or device. [WP-193f](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193f/) records the measurements and unverified limits; [WP-193d](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193d/) retains the earlier feature-only result.

For `task: obb`, the flag records backbone, neck and the complete dual head, including both angle outputs. The native classification and oriented losses stay outside capture. Their empty-target expressions retain zero angle gradients. Overridden training consumers, classification losses or oriented helpers keep the complete native call. The oriented speed-up is likewise limited to a small-batch workload (Nano OBB at batch 4, BF16, one L4): a single batch-8 pair changed fit time by only 4.10%, and replay raised peak reserved memory from 3974 to 4300 MiB, so check throughput and memory on your own batch size. The measurements and remaining limits are in [WP-200](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-200/).

This path requires single-device CUDA automatic optimisation and `task: detect`, `task: keypoints`, `task: obb` or `task: segment`. BF16 replay requires a final PyTorch 2.9 or newer release; 2.9 pre-release and NGC `a0` builds are excluded by design. 2.9 is the first verified runtime: older BF16 runs warn and stay eager because the 2.4 comparison did not meet the exact eager oracle. FP32 and FP16 replay of detection, oriented detection and pose shared features are checked on 2.4 as well; pose stem replay has run on 2.9.1 only ([WP-193f](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193f/)). CPU, MPS and other strategies warn and stay eager; other tasks or `compile_step` raise at construction. One image signature is recorded per fit. A partial batch uses eager execution without growing a graph cache. Changes to the recorded stages’ parameter/buffer storage, module modes, hooks or precision retire replay for the rest of that fit. The supplied network must keep its ordinary stage implementations and static Python configuration. Root forward overrides, stage instance-forward overrides and registered hooks use the eager path. Anomaly detection (`--trainer.detect_anomaly true`) also stays eager so backward NaN checks run normally. A failure while recording raises instead of falling back to eager (RNG state and buffers are restored first), so disable `--model.capture_network` if recording fails on your model. Higher-order differentiation is not supported.

With detection and accumulation one, the module can omit snapshots that the native Lightning automatic-optimization closure clears immediately after forward. The version gate admits Lightning 2.4–2.6; 2.4.0 and 2.6.6 were executed and 2.5.0 was read from source only. Only the inspected native dispatch and pass-through profiler qualify; customized or unsupported contracts retain the snapshots. The module logs once per fit, at rank-zero info level, whether this snapshot-skip fast path is active and, if not, the first check that failed. This is an internal refinement of network replay; there is no additional flag. [WP-193h](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193h/) records the measured workload and verification limits.

Recording warmup restores RNG and BatchNorm buffers before the first real batch. Accumulation or custom optimiser/zero-grad hooks preserve live gradients outside the graph-owned backward buffers before they can be overwritten. AMP uses an uncached autocast scope as the PyTorch API requires. Validation, prediction and public `forward` calls stay eager. Checkpoints retain the ordinary parameter names and the flag, with no graph state. Each fit records afresh and drops its recording on completion or an exception. CUDA graph pools can increase reserved memory even when peak allocated memory falls; measure both on the intended workload. The measured scope and remaining validation gaps are in [WP-193c](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193c/).

For segmentation, the same `--model.capture_network true` option records only backbone and neck. Prediction groups, prototype fusion and both losses keep their existing arithmetic and gradient boundaries. It can combine with `--model.capture_segment_heads true`, which records the prediction groups separately. Overridden or compiled segmentation forwards stay native. The default remains `false`; a recording is transient and follows the same fit cleanup and input-signature rules above. See [WP-193g](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193g/) for the measured workload and limits.

Network replay also shares one current membership traversal between its eligibility and storage checks. Certified scalar module metadata is seeded after recording warmup and reused only while module identities, class forwards, live training modes and ordered attribute bindings are unchanged. Live tensor storage, layout, dtype, gradient flags and hook checks remain independent. This host-bookkeeping change applies whenever `capture_network` replays, independently of `capture_gradient_norm`, without changing the recorded model arithmetic.

## Optional CUDA gradient-norm recording

`--model.capture_gradient_norm true` records PyTorch's global L2 gradient-norm reduction on single-device CUDA automatic optimisation with torch 2.9 or newer. The default is `false`. It is independent of network/loss/update replay and uses the trainer's existing norm clipping configuration, such as `--trainer.gradient_clip_val 10`. Gradient scaling stays in PyTorch's native call and reads the current limit on each step. Disabled clipping (a limit of `None` or at most zero) and value clipping retire recording once with the reason "clipping is disabled or not by norm" and keep the native call. Ordinary `16-mixed` GradScaler training can capture the reduction after unscaling; optimizers that unscale inside their own step (`_step_supports_amp_scaling`, such as fused optimizers) keep the native call, including Lightning's clipping rejection under mixed precision. One gradient shape/stride/dtype/device and stream signature is retained per fit. Offset views and other incompatible gradients or changed public clipping implementations retire recording for that fit. Precision plugins are matched through their type's MRO against stock `Precision`/`MixedPrecision` clipping methods, with each method checked by identity: subclasses inheriting those methods remain eligible; customized module or precision-plugin clipping retires capture with a reason naming the plugin type and keeps the native call. CPU, MPS and unsupported runtimes warn and stay native; the torch gate says the norm decomposition is "verified only on torch>=2.9". Fit completion, failure and copying release the transient recording, which adds no model tensor keys to checkpoints.

Setup and private CUDA buffers have a cost. The 9.55% complete-fit reduction in [WP-200c](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-200c/) covers the whole patch on a pre-integration revision (nano pose/640/BF16, batch 4, L4, five complete pairs), including the network-replay bookkeeping change above. The flag-only share is unmeasured, and the integrated tree was not re-measured. Long-run accuracy remains unverified.

## Optional CUDA detection and pose loss execution

`--model.capture_loss true` replays the existing detection assignment and loss forward/backward with fresh predictions, targets and the current alpha tensor. Default `false`: capture costs setup time and retains CUDA workspace, so short or compute-bound runs may not benefit. It accepts `task: detect` or `task: keypoints`, and requires single-device CUDA automatic optimisation and `compile_step: false`. It can combine with `capture_network`, `capture_orthogonalization` and `capture_updates`; `capture_loss` itself records no optimizer update, so the optimizer step is whatever those two optimizer options select (the existing eager path when both are off).

For pose, the unrotated detection objective uses that recorder while point gathers and OKS stay native. During training, the built-in RLE densities can score both branches in one batch, retaining separate visible-point means and branch weights. That batching is gated on the option being active for the fit, not on the recorder: it continues after the recorder retires and on steps whose detection loss takes its native call, such as a customized criterion or BF16 on torch older than 2.9. This reduces dispatch but can change matrix-kernel selection and parameter-gradient summation rounding: pose execution retains the mathematical objective, but training is not byte-identical. Hooked, overridden or compiled densities, altered pose scoring and validation use their original calls. Branches with different input dtypes/devices or tensor subclasses keep separate density calls. Laplace-only pose keeps native point scoring. See [WP-199b](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-199b/) for the measured scope and unverified accuracy checks.

One masked target workspace grows from observed instance counts and replaces the previous recording. Returned scalars and assignments own their storage. Current label bounds are checked before replay. Global module hooks, unsafe custom epsilon/exponent settings, entirely empty targets, partial batches, non-finite inputs, unsupported layouts or autograd contexts, another CUDA stream and older BF16 runtimes keep the native loss. FP32 and FP16 have focused CUDA coverage on torch 2.4.0 and 2.9.1; BF16 replay starts at the verified final 2.9 runtime. Changed criterion implementations, gains or precision retire the recording. A capture failure raises after clearing the partial owner. Higher-order differentiation and multiple backward passes through one recorded result are outside this automatic-training option.

On the measured L4 nano/640/BF16 workload, five batch-4 complete-fit pairs saved 13.14%. A separate batch-16 exploratory pair was 7.767% slower. Treat this as a small-batch launch-overhead option and measure the complete fit before enabling it for another workload.

[WP-199](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-199/) records the measured workload, discarded screens and remaining validation gaps. Check complete-fit throughput and memory on your own batch size before enabling it.

## CUDA graph replay of orthogonalization

`--model.capture_orthogonalization true` records MuSGD's existing Newton--Schulz matrix calls and replays them with each new gradient. The default is `false`: private graph pools retain extra device workspace, and setup may outweigh the gain on short or compute-bound runs. Momentum, parameter updates and the learning-rate schedule remain eager. CPU and MPS keep the original functions. [WP-197b](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-197b/) records the measured workload and compatibility envelope.

## CUDA update preparation replay

`--model.capture_updates true` additionally records MuSGD's update preparation, including momentum, for eligible dense float32 CUDA groups. Learning-rate changes and parameter writes remain outside capture. This option can be used with or without `capture_orthogonalization`; the two recordings do not nest. CPU, MPS and unsupported CUDA layouts or execution contexts retain the native step. A failure while recording raises instead of falling back to the native step (gradients and momentum are restored first), so disable `--model.capture_updates` if recording fails on your model. Loading optimizer state discards old recordings. The default is `false` because capture adds setup and retains workspace. [WP-197c](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-197c/) reports five complete public-data fits, numerical checks and measured memory cost; other workloads need their own measurement.

## torch.compile (CUDA, detect)

`--model.compile_step true` (or `compile_step: true` under `model:`; `det_nano_smoke.yaml` carries it at `false`) compiles the detection objective with Inductor. What is compiled is one region, `DetectionLitModule._detect_objective`: the forward, both branch decodes, the task-aligned assignment and the dual loss, traced as a single graph with no breaks — `tests/ptl/test_compile.py` pins that on CPU for a batch with ground truths and for one with none. Compiling the model half alone was measured first and was not worth a flag: x1.09–1.16 on the step, because the assignment and the loss are where the small kernels and the launch overhead live. With [WP-183](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-183/)'s dense box terms (no data-dependent gather) and the label check skipped under tracing, the whole region compiles: on an RTX PRO 6000, variant `n`, COCO, batch 16, deterministic, the eager training step is 74.7 ms and the compiled one 60.9 ms, x1.23. A bf16 run was recorded at x1.46 on the same bench and is **not** enabled by this flag — precision is a separate decision the fidelity gate has not been asked about.

What it costs: 110–140 s of compilation per process before the first step, and a handful of recompiles over a run: the training graph, the first `no_grad` evaluation step, and — because Dynamo specialises sizes 0 and 1 whatever is marked — one each for the first batch with no ground truths (`tal.py`'s own branch), the first with exactly one padded instance, and the first with one image, if the loader ever produces it. Measured on CPU with the `eager` backend over five batch shapes: four graphs. Batch size and padded instance count are marked dynamic on the images and the ground truths before every compiled call, so the last, smaller batch of an epoch and a batch with more instances than the one before share one graph; without the marks Dynamo would specialise until `cache_size_limit` (8) and then drop to eager without saying so, and with them the assigner's `F.one_hot(best_gt, num_gt)` — a concrete class count — had to become an `arange` comparison, since the enforcing marks refuse a pinned dim rather than silently recompiling. `TORCH_LOGS=recompiles` shows the count.

Where it refuses, it says so once at `setup` and trains eager. Off CUDA: the MPS Inductor backend crashes in `convolution_backward`, and CPU has nothing to gain. Under `task: segment`, `obb` or `keypoints`: their extra terms read tensors on the host inside `_task_extra_loss`, outside the region, so compiling the detection part alone would buy a fraction of the x1.23 for the same compile cost; they stay eager until their terms are made traceable. The compile wraps the bound method, not the module, so parameter names, the state dict, the EMA shadow, checkpoints and export are exactly what they are without the flag — a compiled *module* would prefix every key with `_orig_mod.`.

The default is off on cost, not on doubt. A78 — whether the compiled objective trains as eager does — was validated on an A100 (paired 4-epoch run: 1 recompile, step 180.6 → 144.2 ms, loss parity `3.6e-5` with TF32 off), but compilation added 210 s of wall to a 4-epoch run of 313 steps, a break-even near 19 epochs at that size and under one epoch on COCO train; turn it on per recipe when the run is long enough. When comparing the two arms, compare mAP, or set `torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("highest")` first: under TF32 the per-batch `train/loss` differs by up to `1e-1`, because the task-aligned assignment is discrete and TF32 rounding moves its top-k set. D24 carries the numbers.

## Lifetime of the replay flags

Each opt-in replay flag is kept or retired on its own record, under the principal's rule P5 ([D32](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/DECISIONS/)). A flag stays while its `make gate-gpu` parity is green and its documented speed-up holds. A flag is retired when its parity stays red past one phase, or when its gain on its documented workload is under 3%. No flag becomes the default in 0.x without a principal call. Nothing on this page is removed by the table below: a flag whose stated gain is already under 3% would be marked as a retirement candidate for the principal, and none is, since every documented-workload figure is well above it. The batch-16 and batch-32 screens quoted elsewhere on this page (2.01% and 2.90% for segmentation, 2.50% for pose features, 4.10% for oriented) are exploratory boundary cases, not the documented workload, and do not trigger the rule.

A known failing CUDA test is a red `main` until it is fixed, and a [GPU] work package does not close without a green `make gate-gpu` run (decision 3 of the 2026-10-20 entry in [ESCALATION](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/ESCALATION/)). A retirement trigger is therefore a call for the principal, not an automatic removal.

| Flag (task) | Work package | Documented workload and measured gain | Keep condition | Retire trigger |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| `capture_network` (detect) | [WP-193c](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193c/) | Nano detection on one L4, torch 2.9.1+cu129: complete-fit median 92.589 s to 77.330 s, 16.48%. | `make gate-gpu` parity green; the gain holds on this workload. | Parity red past one phase, or gain under 3% on this workload. |
| `capture_network` (keypoints) | [WP-193d](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193d/), [WP-193f](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193f/) | Feature replay ([WP-193d](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193d/)), five pairs: complete-fit time falls 11.17%. Stem replay ([WP-193f](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193f/)), nano/640/BF16, batch 4, L4, five pairs: complete runtime falls 12.97%. | Same. | Same. |
| `capture_network` (obb) | [WP-200](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-200/) | Nano oriented, 104 DOTA-v1.0 tiles, eight epochs, batch 4, 1024 px, BF16, one L4, five pairs: complete-fit median drops 12.011% (68.642 s to 60.397 s). | Same. | Same. |
| `capture_network` (segment) | [WP-193g](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193g/) | Nano segmentation, 512 COCO val2017 images, five epochs, batch 4, 640 px, BF16, L4, five pairs, prediction replay already on: complete fit 107.412 s to 87.629 s, 18.42%. | Same. | Same. |
| `capture_loss` (detect) | [WP-199](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-199/) | Nano, batch 4, 640 px, BF16, five epochs on 1,024 COCO val2017 images, L4, five pairs: complete fit 125.272 s to 108.811 s, 13.140%. | Same. | Same. |
| `capture_loss` (keypoints) | [WP-199b](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-199b/) | Registered nano, batch 4, 640 px, BF16, five epochs over 384 COCO person images, L4, five pairs: 100.586 s to 87.058 s, 13.45% less complete-fit time. | Same. | Same. |
| `capture_segment_heads` (segment) | [WP-193e](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193e/) | Nano segmentation, 384 training COCO val2017 images, 10 epochs, batch 4, 640 px, BF16, L4, five pairs: complete fit 202.794 s to 169.130 s, 16.60%. | Same. | Same. |
| `capture_orthogonalization` (MuSGD) | [WP-197b](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-197b/) | Nano detection, first 256 COCO val2017 images, six epochs, batch 4, 640 px, BF16, L4, five pairs: time saved 19.76% on the tree before compatible batching, 12.55% with compatible batching and device HSV applied (expected benefit on current main). | Same. | Same, read against the 12.55% row. |
| `capture_updates` (MuSGD) | [WP-197c](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-197c/) | Nano detection, first 256 COCO val2017 images, ten epochs, batch 4, 640 px, BF16, L4, five pairs: complete fit 120.850 s to 108.750 s, 10.01%. | Same. | Same. |
| `compile_step` (detect) | WP-184 ([roadmap row](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/ROADMAP/), D24 in [Decisions](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/DECISIONS/)) | Measured x1.23 on the detect step, RTX PRO 6000, variant `n`, COCO, batch 16; 110–140 s compile per process. WP-184 has no page of its own, so this is the roadmap row's figure, a step-time ratio rather than a complete-fit time. | Same; the compile cost is paid per process. | Same, with the step-time ratio converted to a complete-fit gain. |

Every row's "gain" is the figure its page states for the workload shown, on one device; none is a claim for another batch size, device or full-COCO run. The pose-feature row is not a complete-fit figure for the stem replay alone: [WP-193f](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-193f/) measures stem replay against feature replay already enabled.

# 📚 Provenance Log

Every design decision in this repository cites its public source. This file is the clean-room evidence record: sources are logged here on first use, and every commit carries a `Provenance:` trailer referencing the source ids below. No Ultralytics code surface, config, weight, or web property (including docs.ultralytics.com) has been consulted at any point — see the denylist in AGENTS.md.

## ✅ Source allowlist

Admissible references. Anything not on this list requires a DECISIONS.md entry before first use; denylisted surfaces are never admissible.

Reference *implementations* (R25–R28, R36) are admitted under D13/ADR-004 on two standing conditions. **Licence:** MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause or ISC only — copyleft (AGPL, GPL, LGPL), source-available, research-only, non-commercial, commercially licensed and unlicensed code are inadmissible at any cost, and an unestablished licence counts as inadmissible rather than permissive. **Use:** reading for diagnosis only; copying code from any external detection repository remains prohibited (AGENTS.md sec. 7). A per-use provenance check still applies to individual files — the entries below record licence verification, not a blanket clearance of every file in the repository.

The row named `0a0cc640` until [WP-146](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-146/) reconciled it with `pyproject.toml`, which has pinned `fedde0c1` since [WP-132](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-132/). That bump is not fixture-neutral, and `0a0cc640` is the whole of why: it redefines `GeomShape.TRIANGLE` from equilateral to obtuse-scalene and re-centres every outline on its area centroid, moving the det/obb/seg fixtures' instance counts and box sums ([WP-132](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-132/)'s log carries the deltas and what was re-frozen). `fedde0c1` is fixture-neutral, measured rather than assumed — both generator-derived goldens produce identical values at either commit ([WP-146](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-146/)). Advanced from `fedde0c1` to `a5a276a` (the tree upstream tags `v0.12.0` from) by [WP-154](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-154/), which the Phase 14 augmentation upstreaming is gated on; this bump spans fifteen upstream commits of which only two touch the generator. `964fd07` (registry, SVG assets, `Fill` type) removes the `animal_shapes` helper — replaced here by the `tuple(AnimalShape)[:n]` selection it performed — and is fixture-neutral, measured at the commit. `abbf1f2` (upright OBB, triangle) is the whole of what moves: `PrimitiveShape.TRIANGLE` becomes equilateral again and `polygon_to_obb` is re-derived in the shape's upright frame instead of by minimum-area calipers, returning all sixteen moved golden values bit-exactly to the figures frozen before `0a0cc640` ([WP-154](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-154/)'s log carries the per-commit trace). The remaining eleven commits are augmentation-engine work and move no fixture value. No YOLO-implementation lineage; verified Apache-2.0 |

Not an external source and not admissible as one: this row exists because the register is what a reader checks a citation against, and a document cited 133 times from `src/` with no row here is a citation that resolves to nothing.

It states the layout (sec. 7), the variant table (sec. 5.1, itself sourced from R3 Fig. 1), the block stack (sec. 5.2, 5.3), the loss composition (sec. 5.7), the augmentation recipe (sec. 5.9), the dataset layout (sec. 14.3) and D1–D11, which `docs/DECISIONS.md` transcribes. Cited from code by section: 133 `blueprint` references across 36 files under `src/`, 107 of them in the `blueprint sec. N` form (measured 2026-09-05). **Every method claim it carries is downstream of R1–R36** — where a blueprint section and a paper disagree the paper governs, and where the blueprint is the only source the choice is an assumption and belongs in `ASSUMPTIONS.md`. Registered by [WP-175](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-175/); the amendments made after it are D12. |

## 🏷️ Naming evidence record

Package name `lucid-yolo` uses "YOLO" as a model-family/category term. Evidence:

1. **Origin**: "YOLO" coined by Redmon et al. (2016) [R20]; the original Darknet implementations are MIT-licensed.
2. **Multi-party generic usage**: YOLOX (Megvii), YOLOv6 (Meituan), YOLOv7/v9 (Wang et al.), PP-YOLOE (Baidu), YOLO-NAS (Deci), YOLOv13 (Lei et al.) — a decade of unrelated parties using the family name.
3. **Ultralytics' own position** \[R19\]: licensing terms "apply to the specific implementation of the YOLO models, not the conceptual model itself."
4. **Word-mark status**: the bare "YOLO" US software word mark is registered to an unrelated entity (Next Computer Inc., Reg. 6927573), itself subject to a pending cancellation proceeding.

**Usage discipline** — the rule cited across this repository as *sec. 3.5*. This document carries no section numbers, so that citation resolves to nothing on its own; it is recorded here, at the paragraph it names, so the existing citations resolve rather than being rewritten one by one. Cite it as `PROVENANCE.md`'s usage discipline in anything written from now on.

"YOLO26", "YOLO11", "Ultralytics", and their logos never appear in package names, module paths, class names, or model identifiers. Nominative references to the paper ("the YOLO26 paper, arXiv:2606.03748") are the only usage. The YOLO26 method implementation is exposed under the feature name `e2e` (variants `lucid-yolo-e2e-{n,s,m,l,x}`), never a version number.

## 📝 Usage log

First-use log of sources consulted during implementation. Papers are cited by arXiv id; access dates recorded per session.

**Two properties of this table a reader should not have to infer.** It is a *first-use* log, not a coverage index: a source appears once, on the day it was first read, and every later use of it is traced through the `Provenance:` trailers and the register rows above rather than by another line here. And it has lagged the allowlist — the rows below were reconciled against the register on 2026-09-06, which added every source that had been registered without a usage line and marked the ones with no consultation to record. Registration and use are different acts, and this table only ever recorded the second; where it recorded neither, that was the defect, not evidence of a quiet read.

The `R1–R20` row is a genuine collapse and stays one. Those twenty were transcribed into the policy documents in a single seeding pass (WP-003) from the blueprint's own reference list, not read one at a time, so splitting the row into twenty dated lines would invent twenty first-use events that never happened. Which of them a given decision actually rests on is in the register's Role column and in each commit's trailer, and that is the resolution this table cannot supply.

# 📋 Assumption Register

Anywhere the papers underdetermine the implementation, the chosen assumption, its public source, and its validation plan are recorded here **before** the corresponding code lands. Rule: any new gap discovered during implementation gets an entry before the code merges. Assumption revisions after a release ship as PATCH (if within golden tolerances) or the next 0.MINOR (if results move).

**Adding a row also raises the floor.** `_ASSUMPTION_FLOOR` in `scripts/lint/audit_docs_present.py` counts the rows this register is allowed to hold and never fall below; the `docs-present` hook reports a shrink against it. It is a ratchet: raise it to the new row count in the same commit that adds the row, never lower it. `_DECISION_FLOOR` (`DECISIONS.md`) and `_WP_FLOOR` (`ROADMAP.md`) work the same way and want the same edit. The floor sat at 26 against 73 rows until [WP-168](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-168/), which is 47 rows of slack — a register can only be certified by a number somebody keeps current.

Status legend, **rewritten 2026-09-06 to describe what the column actually holds** — the previous wording defined `revised` as "superseded" and `validated` as "validation plan executed and passed", and the register contradicts both:

- `open` — the assumption governs, and the evidence that would settle it is not in yet: either the code has not landed, or the validation it names needs a run nobody has done. Not "unused": most `open` rows are shipping code.
- `active` — in the codebase, with its validation plan run as far as an offline gate can take it.
- `validated` — reserved for the rows whose validation was a *measurement against an independent oracle or a paired run*, rather than a unit test that pins the choice. It is a strong claim and only a handful of rows carry it.
- `revised` — the assumption's **value** changed after code shipped against the old one, and the row is the current one either way. It does **not** mean superseded: the sole row carrying it is in force today. Most revisions do not use this status at all — a revised row usually keeps `active` or `open` and records the change inline, dated, in its own Assumption cell.

Two consequences of that last point, both load-bearing when reading the column: **a row's status does not tell you whether it has been revised** (several `active` and `open` rows carry dated inline revisions, and several say VALIDATED inline while staying `active`), and **the four statuses are not a lifecycle** — nothing progresses `open → active → validated` on a schedule. Read the Assumption and Validation cells; the status is a coarse filter, not a summary. Counts are deliberately not stated here: they move with every row that lands, and a tally written into prose is the thing that goes stale — `scripts/lint/audit_docs_present.py` is what counts the register, and it counts rows rather than statuses.

| ID | Gap in papers | Assumption | Public source | Validation | Status |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| A1 | Box IoU loss variant unnamed | CIoU | R9, R10 | Ablation-neutral check at the smoke tier | open |
| A2 | TAL alpha/beta not restated | alpha=1, beta=6 | R4 | Overfit + ablations-tier trend | open |
| A3 | C3k2/C2PSA sub-block internals beyond Fig. S2 | Bottleneck/PSA internals per YOLO11 lineage; nested `C3k` inner-bottleneck count **1** (`_C3K_INNER_UNITS`, revised 2026-08-01 from 2 by [WP-023](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-023/) iteration 2 — at depth=1.0 the `l`/`x` variants carry two nested units per `c3k=True` stage and `n=2` overshot the R1 Table 7 FLOP budget; `n=1` lands all five scales within +/-5% FLOPs while keeping params within +/-2%) | R11, R1 Fig. S2 | Param/FLOP gate (Phase 2) — `tests/models/test_param_flops.py::test_det_vs_table7` passes all 5 scales | active |
| A4 | SPPF shortcut exact form | Input added to output of pooling stack | R3 sec. 4 | Param gate; ablate if mismatch | open |
| A5 | Newton–Schulz iteration count | 5 | R7, R8 | Orthogonality unit test | open |
| A6 | Muon step scaling | 0.2 * sqrt(max(A,B)) update-RMS scaling | R7 Eq. 4 (verbatim: 0.2 * O * sqrt(max(A,B))) | Toy convergence test | active |
| A7 | muon_w+sgd_w != 1 semantics | Independent additive gains | R1 Tables S4/S7 | Documented; sensitivity note | open |
| A8 | LR schedule shape (lrf semantics) | Per-step linear decay to final LR = lr0\*lrf, preceded by a linear warmup over `warmup_epochs` (default 3) from `lr0/warmup_steps` (revised 2026-08-03 by WP-072: warmup added — Det-smoke attempt 1 ran the constant-LR deferral and plateaued at val mAP50-95 3.96 vs the >25 criterion; overfit-100 golden keeps the schedule off, `lrf: 1.0`/`warmup_epochs: 0`) | gap; decay convention widely restated in third-party YOLO-application literature; warmup is generic from-scratch practice (A31 lineage) | `tests/optim/test_schedule.py` endpoints; **Det-smoke attempt 3 VALIDATED 2026-08-06** (warmup + decay to lr0\*lrf over the full 50-epoch budget, monotonic val descent, acceptance met); trend-neutral in paired ablations-tier runs | active |
| A9 | One-to-one output tuple (...,6) | [x1,y1,x2,y2,score,class]; seg appends K coefficients | R1 sec. 3.2.1 | Eval round-trip test | open |
| A10 | Resize semantics | Letterbox, aspect-preserving. Since [WP-155](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-155/) the fit, the forward matrix and the resample are R21's — `letterbox_geometry`, `letterbox_matrix`, and a letterbox-only `Compose` segment that runs one `grid_sample` from the source canvas to the letterboxed one in place of an `F.interpolate` followed by an `F.pad`. What this row is actually about stays local: `Letterbox.forward_affine` and `Letterbox.inverse_map` keep their signatures and their semantics, and the inverse stays closed-form (`inv_r`, `-pad * inv_r`) rather than a numerical inversion of the forward matrix, because the round trip below has to be **exact** and a numerical inversion leaves a residual in it. Delegating moved pixels and not geometry, which is the whole content of the boundary here: `letterbox_image_mean` moved 0.5024 → 0.4994 and not one coordinate golden did (measured and re-frozen by WP-155b) | YOLO-lineage convention in third-party literature (e.g. R11); the letterbox segment itself is R21 (ADR-005) | Bbox/mask round-trip test — `tests/data/test_letterbox.py` | open |
| A11 | Anchor center placement | (i+0.5)\*stride | R4, R5 | Assignment unit test | open |
| A12 | Weight-decay exclusions | 1D params excluded | Standard practice (e.g. R7 discussion) | Documented | open |
| A13 | From-scratch loss gains; coordinate frame of the L1 term the legacy DFL gain field scales | Pretrain-style gains (7.5/0.5/6.0); the L1 term is measured in **stride units** — the head's native ltrb parameterization — not pixels (revised 2026-08-04 by WP-078: with pixel-frame L1 the term ran 8-32x large and was 97.4% of the val objective at Det-smoke attempt 2's endpoint, starving classification — mAP50-95 6.3, mar_100 24% despite well-localized boxes; decomposition arithmetic reproduces the logged 200.7 val total exactly) | R1 Table S2; head ltrb frame per R4/R6 lineage | `test_detection_loss.py::test_l1_stride_normalization_divides_by_anchor_stride`; **Det-smoke attempt 3 VALIDATED 2026-08-06** — stride-frame L1 moved classification from 1.7% to 23.0% of the objective and val mAP50-95 from 6.28 to 25.30 at half the epoch budget | active |
| A14 | Prototype count K | K=32 | YOLACT R16 | Param/FLOP gate vs Table S9 | open |
| A15 | Proto spatial resolution | 160x160 at 640 input (2x upsample of P3) | YOLACT convention R16 | Param/FLOP gate; mask-quality check | open |
| A16 | Coefficient activation + instance-mask loss | tanh coefficients; per-pixel BCE on box-cropped masks, box-area normalized | YOLACT R16 | Overfit micro-set mask IoU | open |
| A17 | Aux semantic head structure | A single 1x1 `nn.Conv2d` from the fused-feature width (`ProtoFusion.out_channels`) to `nc` raw logits, evaluated at `F_proto`'s own resolution with no resampling, carrying the A30 prior-probability bias init (it is a dense sigmoid classifier over a mostly-background map — exactly A30's setting, unlike the tanh coefficient stems). `forward` returns `None` whenever `self.training` is False — keyed on module mode, never on grad mode — so the branch is provably absent at eval and export, and the fused-parameter gate has exactly one convolution to account for | R1 sec. 3.4.1 ("training-only branch") | Fused-model param gate proves removal; `tests/models/test_aux_semantic.py` pins the eval-mode `None`, the single-conv parameter count, and the prior init | active |
| A18 | Proto-generation stack internals | Three 3x3 ConvBNAct units at the fusion width, 2x nearest upsample, one 3x3 ConvBNAct, 1x1 convolution to K raw prototypes | YOLACT R16; R1 Eq. 9 | Param/FLOP gate | active |
| A19 | Rotated IoU loss variant | ProbIoU | R1 sec. 3.4.3 lineage; R17 | OBB-ablations trend (Table 11 ranking) | open |
| A20 | Angle branch structure **and hidden width** (R1 sec. 3.4.3 says only "separate branch ... to predict the orientation angle"; Fig. S2 draws one stem shape and no widths, and Table S11 reports whole-model sizes from which a branch width can only be inferred) | A third per-level stem beside the box and class stems on **each** head branch, shaped like them — two depthwise-separable units then a 1x1 — and emitting **one** scalar per location. Widened 2026-08-11 by [WP-062](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-062/): the hidden width is `max(16, channels // 2)` (`_angle_stem_width`), **not** A28's shared `max(16, channels // 3)`, which the Table S11 gate rejected. Both divisors were measured on all five scales as the ratio of the isolated angle-branch cost to the increment Table S11 implies over Table 7 once the 80-to-15 class saving is credited back — `// 3`: n 0.76, s 0.98, m 0.66, l 0.66, x 0.63; `// 2`: n 1.22, s 1.62, m 1.09, l 1.09, x 1.04. Table S11 rounds params to 0.1 M, so that implied increment carries +/-59% at n and +/-21% at s and neither scale can discriminate; at m and l (+/-8%) and x (+/-3.5%) it can, and it selects `// 2`. **Neither divisor is uniformly right** — `// 3` undershoots the three large scales, `// 2` overshoots s at 1.62 — so the published angle cost is not one fixed fraction of the level width, and this row stays `open`: a rule chosen where the evidence is sharp, not a claim of Table S11 parity | R1 sec. 3.4.3 ("separate branch"), R1 Fig. S2 (stem shape); the width itself: gap, inferred from R1 Table S11 | `test_param_flops.py::test_obb_vs_tableS11` at the table's 1024 px and 15 classes (params +/-3.5%, FLOPs +/-5%); `test_obb_head.py::test_angle_stem_parameter_count_exact` pins each level term by term, `::test_angle_branch_uses_wider_stem_than_box_and_class_stems` pins the split against being tidied away | open |
| A21 | DOTA crop overlap (R1 sec. 4.5.3 says only "overlapping 1024x1024 crops") | Overlap is a **parameter** of `tile_windows`, defaulting to the 200 px this row has recorded since the register was written, so the assumption still governs. Flagged 2026-08-11 by [WP-057](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-057/): 200 px is attested by **neither** cited source — R18 sec. 4 publishes its own protocol as 1024 px patches "with a stride set to 512", i.e. a 512 px overlap, and R13 (MMRotate, arXiv:2204.13317) fixes the long-edge-135 angle definition but names no crop overlap at all. The value is therefore a **sensitivity item for the OBB tier**: re-running the tier at overlap 512 against the default 200 is the check that settles it. Window placement is overlap-agnostic by construction — the last window of each axis sits flush against the far edge — so full coverage holds for any overlap in `[0, patch)` and the sweep costs only tiles, not code | R18 sec. 4 (1024 px patch, stride 512); R13 (angle definition only, no overlap); the 200 px value itself: gap | `tests/data/test_tiling.py::test_coverage_no_gaps` — no-gap coverage over sizes that divide evenly, leave a remainder or are shorter than the patch, including the A21 defaults on a DOTA-sized image; OBB-tier sensitivity run pending ([WP-063](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-063/)/088) | active |
| A22 | Scalar weight of R1 Eq. 15's angle term in the total objective (R1 states the term and its internal `lambda`, but never its weight against the box and classification terms) | **0.25**, revised 2026-08-12 by [WP-093](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-093/) from the 1.0 this project assumed. The inherited value does not merely underperform, it *destabilises*: on the oriented overfit slice at 100 epochs across five seeds, `angle_gain = 1.0` cleared the 0.9 floor on 1 of 5 with a run-to-run spread of 0.667 and a worst seed of 0.3077, while `0.25` cleared 4 of 5 with spread 0.096. Mean angular error on elongated targets halves, 25.47 to 11.85 degrees. The failure is specific and mechanical: `sin^2(2 d_theta)` is zero at **both** 0 and 90 degrees, so for an elongated box the term scores a quarter turn as perfect and only the rotated IoU term objects, and its gradient `2 sin(4 d_theta)` reverses at 45 degrees. R1 intends this to be harmless — "elongated boxes receive smaller omega_i and remain primarily constrained by the rotated IoU loss" — but at the paper's own `lambda = 3` a 2:1 box still carries `omega = 0.948`, a five percent reduction, so the stated intent is not delivered by the stated formula in that band. The remedy is this gain and **not** `lambda`, which R1 does state and ablates (Table 11: `lambda = 5` scores worse than omitting the term entirely). Dose-response is not monotone per seed — seed 3 is best at 1.0 and worst at 0.5 — which is why a gain was chosen on aggregate behaviour rather than by picking the best-looking seed | R1 Eq. 15 (the term and `lambda`); the weight itself: gap | `test_obb_training.py::test_angle_gain_default_registered_a22_value` pins the value, since every other test passes gains explicitly and the default was previously unread. Measured lead-side, 35 training runs over four paired campaigns, five seeds each: gains 1.0 / 0.5 / 0.25 / 0.0 cleared 1 / 4 / 4 / 5 of 5 with mean elongated angular error 25.47 / 19.09 / 11.85 / 12.49 degrees. Still open at the OBB-smoke and DOTA tiers, where aspect ratios reach 5:1 and 10:1 and `omega` genuinely falls (0.750, 0.555) — the regime this fixture's 2:1 targets do not cover | revised |
| A23 | Rotated decode normalization (R1 Eq. 13 makes the predicted angle the raw pre-activation, so the head can emit any real number at any magnitude, and R1 never says where that number is brought back into a range) | Normalization happens **after** the decode, not in the head: `decode_rboxes` ends in `rotated_geom.canonicalize`, returning the unique long-edge representative with `w >= h` and theta on `[-pi/4, 3*pi/4)` (R13's long-edge-135 definition, [WP-055](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-055/)'s conventions). Two consequences are deliberate. The **dense** `(B, A, 5)` output is canonicalized rather than only the ranked detections, so a caller that decodes without ranking — a loss, an assigner, an export graph — cannot reach an un-normalized angle by a shorter path. And because theta and theta + pi describe the same rectangle, the decode is continuous across that identification: two raw values a half turn apart yield the same box rather than two boxes | R13 (angle definition); the placement after the decode: gap | `test_obb_head.py::test_decode_canonicalizes_adversarial_raw_angles` over raw magnitudes far outside any range, `::test_decode_continuous_across_half_turn_identification`, `::test_angle_output_unsquashed_beyond_legacy_range` (100 radians out of the stem, evidence the Eq. 12 squashing is gone rather than merely unobserved) | active |
| A24 | Rotated evaluation IoU and its scoring protocol (R1 Tables 10-11 report rotated mAP50-95 on DOTA-v1.0 val and define neither the IoU, the matching rule, the recall interpolation, the detection cap nor the class-averaging convention) | Exact polygon intersection: Sutherland-Hodgman clipping of one quadrilateral against the other plus the shoelace area, vectorized in torch on `rboxes_to_polygons` corners (`eval/dota_eval.py`, [WP-063](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-063/)). Clipping is edge-inclusive, matching [WP-055](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-055/)'s `points_in_rboxes` (A25); a shared edge or corner bounds zero area and scores 0 either way. Working dtype follows the input — no float64, because evaluation runs on MPS, the constraint A41 records for ProbIoU. Conditioning is fixed structurally instead: IoU is translation-invariant, so each pair is re-centred on its own midpoint **before** its corners are expanded. The order is load-bearing and measured — worst error against a float64 shapely evaluation over 300 overlapping pairs is 1.4e-07 at every offset from 0 to 1e6 when re-centring precedes expansion, against 2.7e-05 at 1e4 and 1.4e-03 at 1e6 when it follows. Zero-area, negative-extent and reversed-winding boxes clamp to zero area and yield IoU 0 rather than NaN. Averaging follows R12's COCO conventions: ten thresholds 0.50 to 0.95 step 0.05, classes without ground truth excluded from the mean — refined to **non-difficult** ground truth, an all-difficult class having an empty recall denominator. Reported as `map`, `map_50`, `map_75`, `mar_300`, the first three sharing `coco_eval.py`'s names. The small/medium/large breakdown is deliberately absent: COCO's area ranges are an R12 constant with no oriented counterpart, and inventing one would be a threshold without a source | R18 sec. 4 and its devkit (difficult convention); R12 (threshold grid, zero-GT exclusion); R13 (long-edge convention); R31 (the oracle); the polygon kernel and the re-centring order: gap | `tests/eval/test_dota_eval.py::TestRotatedIou::test_vs_oracle` — 600 random pairs across the canonical angle range against a shapely oracle at 1e-4, half near-coincident so the near-parallel regime is reached; `::test_vs_oracle_edge_cases` covers 15 named pairs including both range bounds of the square fold, zero-area and degenerate lines; lead-side re-measurement with the oracle reading back the same float32 values the kernel receives, holding 1.4e-07 to 2.3e-07 at offsets 0, 1e3, 1e4 and 1e6. OBB-tier confirmation pending [WP-088](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-088/) | active |
| A25 | STAL/TAL containment for rotated GT (R1 sec. 3.3.3 states STAL generically over box dimensions and never restates it for oriented boxes) | Point-in-rotated-rect containment, edge-inclusive, inherited from `points_in_rboxes`; the STAL clamp applied to the rotated `(w, h)` at the same `s_min = 8`, `s_ref = 16` the axis-aligned path uses, R1 giving no separate oriented thresholds. **Revised 2026-08-11 ([WP-061](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-061/))** with two scoping facts the original wording left implicit and that are now load-bearing: the rotated box decides **candidacy only** — the IoU, the alignment metric `t = s^alpha · u^beta`, `target_boxes` and `align_weights` all keep running on the axis-aligned `gt_boxes`, so entry `(b, n)` of the two must describe the same object and the oriented path is **not** end-to-end until rotated IoU lands in the metric ([WP-062](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-062/)/088); and `gt_rboxes` is per call rather than per GT, so a batch is wholly oriented or wholly axis-aligned, an axis-aligned object inside an oriented batch encoding as `theta = 0` | R1 sec. 3.3.3 (generic formulation); the oriented reading and the carried-over thresholds: gap | `test_rotated_assign.py::test_tiny_rotated_gt` (a 6x6 GT at 45 deg: vanilla TAL 0 candidates, STAL 4), `::test_rotation_excludes_envelope_corners` (a 16x16 GT at 45 deg drops the four envelope corners the axis-aligned test keeps), `::test_axis_aligned_assignment_bit_identical`. | A28 | Detection-head stem structure and hidden width (Fig. S2 shows the stem pair, not widths) | Both box and class stems are **depthwise-separable** (two `DepthwiseConv+ConvBNAct` units + 1x1 output), shared hidden width `max(16, channels // 3)` (`_stem_width`); no `num_classes` floor ([WP-023](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-023/) iteration 1). Revised 2026-08-01 from the original full-conv box stem (`channels // 4`, two `3x3` convs) + class stem (`max(num_classes, channels // 2)`): the [WP-023](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-023/) param gate flagged the head as ~7-16x the reference budget (the box stem alone was ~3.7x the class stem despite emitting 4 vs `num_classes` channels, and the `num_classes` floor bloated the `n`/`s` head). | A29 | R1 Table 7 param/FLOP counting convention | GFLOPs = **2x** fvcore MACs (conventional one-multiply-plus-one-add FLOPs; raw MACs land ~48% low). **Params** count the full trained checkpoint (both dual-head branches); **FLOPs** count the deployed NMS-free inference model only (backbone+neck+one-to-one head — the one-to-many branch is training-only and never executed at E2E inference). | A26 | Blueprint prescribes hand-annotated permissive fixture images; none exist | Test fixtures AND [DATA]-WP stand-ins are generated synthetically with fuse-augmentations (R21), seeded. | A33 | Batch transport precision unspecified (R1 silent; engineering-efficiency secondary goal) | Collated image batches cross the DataLoader worker boundary quantized to **uint8** (`round(x*255)`; restored `code/255` on the destination device at the consumer's precision) — post-augmentation pixels rounded to `1/255` steps, worst-case round-trip error `1/510`. Per-sample pipeline numerics (and the data goldens, measured pre-collate) unchanged. **Opt-in exception, `--data.device_hsv` (CUDA with float32 or mixed precision, [WP-197](https://borda.github.io/lucid-YOLO/work_packages/wp-197/))**: workers defer the HSV colour transform, so deferred batches cross the worker boundary as float32 images with the drawn gains, at four times the default image IPC; the consumer applies the batched HSV, then quantizes onto the same `1/255` grid and restores its dtype.
